title: How Much Does a Website Cost in India? 2026 Price Guide
description: What a business website costs in India in 2026: one-time and monthly prices, the yearly running costs, what changes a quote, and what to ask before paying.
content:
Ask five web designers what a website costs and you will hear five numbers, from a few thousand rupees to a few lakh. The spread is not random. It comes from a handful of decisions you can make yourself once you know what they are.

This guide covers those decisions, the costs that come back every year, and our own prices as a worked example, so you can read any quote line by line. Prices were checked in October 2026.

The short answer

For a small business in India, these are sensible starting points. The figures are ours, as one example of how a studio prices the work:

  • A one-page website (a landing page): from ₹8,000, paid once.
  • A website of several pages: ₹12,000 to ₹25,000, paid once.
  • A website on a monthly plan: ₹899/month + ₹2,999 one-time setup, on a 12-month plan, for a site on one of our ready designs.
  • A portal or web app with logins, fee records or bookings: ₹40,000 to ₹85,000, paid once.

On top of a one-time build you pay for your domain and hosting every year. GST is not applicable on our prices: we are not registered under GST, so the price shown is the full amount you pay.

What decides the price

1. How many pages, and what kind

A one-page site that says who you are, what you offer, where you are and how to reach you is the cheapest useful website. Every extra page adds design, writing and testing time. A clinic with a page for each treatment, or a coaching institute with a page for each course, needs more pages than a shop that sells one thing.

2. A ready design or a custom one

A ready design is a layout that already exists, adapted with your logo, colours, text and photos. A custom design is drawn for you, page by page, with rounds of revisions. Custom costs more because the design stage is real work. Both can look professional, so ask to see the design before you pay the balance.

3. Features beyond pages

An enquiry form, a WhatsApp button and a map are standard. A booking form, a Hindi version, a notices section you update yourself or a downloadable fee structure all add time. Logins for parents, students or patients, online payments and stored records are a different kind of project: that is a portal, and it is priced as one.

4. Content: who writes it and who shoots it

Text, photos and translation are the most underestimated part of any website. Many studios, including us, do not include writing or photography: you send the text and photos, and they are put in place. If a quote looks unusually low, check whether it assumes finished text and photos from you.

5. Who builds it

You can build it yourself on a website builder, hire a freelancer or hire a studio: you are trading your own time and risk against money. The questions further down work for all three.

Costs that come back every year

A website is not only a build. Plan for these running costs:

  • Domain name. Your web address, renewed every year with the registrar. Register it in your own name, on your own account, and check the renewal price as well as the first-year offer.
  • Hosting and SSL. The server your site runs on, and the padlock in the address bar. On a one-time build with us you buy hosting in your own name. On our monthly plans, hosting and SSL are included.
  • Business email, if you want it. An address like contact@yourclinic.in. Some providers have a free tier: Zoho Mail's Forever Free plan, for example, covers one domain for up to 5 users with 5 GB of mail storage each, without IMAP or POP access, according to Zoho's pricing page.
  • Changes after launch. Fees, timings, notices and photos change. On a one-time site you update the editable parts yourself or pay for help; our care plans start at ₹1,000 a month. Our monthly plans include 2 content changes a month on Starter and 5 on Growth.
  • Optional extras. SMS or WhatsApp message credits, payment gateway charges, and local SEO if you want help showing up on Google Maps. Ours is from ₹4,999 a month, and no ranking is promised.

Our prices, as one worked example

What you getPrice (October 2026)
Landing page: one page with an enquiry formFrom ₹8,000, one time
Website: several pages and an enquiry form₹12,000 to ₹25,000, one time
Starter plan: a ready design, up to 5 pages, WhatsApp button, hosting and SSL, 2 content changes a month₹899/month + ₹2,999 one-time setup, 12-month plan
Growth plan: everything in Starter, plus a page for each treatment, course or service, a booking or enquiry form, a Hindi version and 5 content changes a month₹1,999/month + ₹2,999 one-time setup, 12-month plan
Portal or web app: records, logins, payments₹40,000 to ₹85,000, one time

First-year totals on the monthly plans: ₹13,787 on Starter (₹2,999 + 12 × ₹899) and ₹26,987 on Growth (₹2,999 + 12 × ₹1,999). One-time projects are paid 50% in advance and 50% at launch, and the custom code is yours on the final payment. GST not applicable: we are not registered under GST. Every package, and what it includes, is on our pricing page.

How to compare two quotes

Put the quotes side by side and ask each provider the same questions. The answers matter more than the totals.

  1. Is there a written scope, with a list of what is not included?
  2. How many rounds of revisions are included, and what does another round cost?
  3. Is the domain registered in your name, on your own account?
  4. Who pays for hosting, in whose name, and what does it cost from the second year?
  5. Can you change simple things yourself, such as timings or a notice? If not, who does it, and at what price?
  6. When do you get the code? On a monthly plan, what is the buy-out price?
  7. What happens after launch, and for how long are defects fixed free? Ours is 30 days.
  8. Does anyone promise you a Google ranking? Treat that as a warning sign. Google's own guidance says: "No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google."

Which option fits which business

  • Just starting, small budget: a landing page, or the Starter plan if you would rather spread the cost.
  • A clinic, school or coaching institute with several services: a multi-page website, or the Growth plan with a page for each treatment or course. See what we include for dental clinics, schools and coaching institutes.
  • You need logins, fee records or online payments: a portal.

If you cannot decide between paying once and paying monthly, we compared the two in Monthly website plan or one-time payment, and the plan itself is explained on our monthly website plan page.

Questions people ask

Can I get a business website for under ₹10,000?

Yes. A one-page landing page starts at ₹8,000 with us. On the Starter plan you pay ₹3,898 to start (the ₹2,999 one-time setup plus the first month), then ₹899 a month for the rest of the 12-month plan, ₹13,787 in the first year. A multi-page site with a custom design costs more.

Do I have to pay for a website every year?

For the domain, yes, and for hosting on a one-time build. On a monthly plan, hosting is part of the monthly fee, but you still renew the domain yourself with the registrar.

Why do quotes for the same website vary so much?

Because they rarely describe the same website. Line them up on pages, design, features, content and exclusions. Once those match, what is left is the provider's time and support.

How long does a website take?

A landing page or a small website takes a few weeks of working time. With us the clock starts when the advance has cleared and your text and photos are with us, and each package on our pricing page shows its working weeks.

Want a price for your own site? Send us a message with what you do and where, and we will reply with a written scope and a fixed price. Or start from website options by type of business.

title: Dental Clinic Website: What It Must Have (2026 Checklist)
description: What patients look for on a dental clinic website, what the Dental Council of India's code allows on it, and a page-by-page checklist for clinics in India.
content:
Picture a patient with a toothache on a weekday evening. She searches on her phone and opens a few clinic websites. On each one she is checking three things: is this clinic near me, does it do what I need, and can I trust it?

A good dental clinic website answers those three questions on the first screen, then makes booking easy. Below is a page-by-page checklist, and the rules in the Dental Council of India's code of ethics that decide what a clinic may say on its own website.

What the Dental Council of India allows on a clinic website

Dentists in India follow the Revised Dentists (Code of Ethics) Regulations, 2014. They allow a clinic website, with conditions. Clause 8.2.9 says that maintaining a website "where all information is factual will not be construed as unethical practice", and that websites "can also carry details of treatment facilities available and the fees for the same". The same clause adds that websites "should not make claims or statements that are not factual and therefore misleading to the public".

In practice, that means:

  • Facts, not superlatives. For listings on the internet, the code treats "any claim to superiority or special skills over others" as unethical (clause 8.2.8), and when a clinic announces new equipment or services it rules out "boastful claims of being the 'best' or 'first'" (clause 8.2.7). "Best dental clinic in Delhi" does not belong on your site.
  • Specialist titles only with the qualification. The code bars a dentist from claiming to be a specialist on the name board or stationery without a special qualification in that specialty recognised by the Council (clause 8.3.3), and the same care makes sense on a website.
  • Fees are allowed. Clause 8.2.9 allows fees on the website, and clause 5.7.1 says there is no bar on displaying fees and other charges in the clinic.
  • Care with case photos and stories. The code says a dentist shall not "boast of cases, operations, cures or remedies" (clause 8.2). Ask your own adviser before you publish before-and-after photos or patient stories, and never publish a patient's photo or name without their written consent.
  • Care with your own photograph. The code calls printing a self-photograph on a letterhead or a clinic signboard self-advertisement (clause 8.3.1). It does not mention websites, so ask your adviser how you want to show the dentists.

This is a summary for planning a website, not legal advice. Read the regulations yourself, or ask someone qualified, before you publish.

The first screen: three answers and three buttons

On a phone, before any scrolling, a patient should see:

  • The clinic's name and a plain description, such as "Family dental clinic in Malviya Nagar".
  • Today's timings, and whether you see walk-ins or appointments only.
  • A call button, a WhatsApp button and a "Book an appointment" button.
  • The locality, with a link that opens the clinic in Google Maps.

The pages a dental clinic website needs

  1. Home. The first screen above, your main treatments, the dentists, and your address.
  2. A page for each main treatment. Root canal treatment, implants, braces and aligners, cleaning, extraction, children's dentistry: whichever you offer. Say what the treatment is, who it is for, how many visits it usually takes at your clinic, what recovery is like, and the fee or fee range if you publish one.
  3. The dentists. Each dentist's name, degrees as registered, the treatments they do and the days they are at the clinic. Specialist titles only where the qualification supports them.
  4. Fees, or how you give estimates. The code allows fees on your website. If the cost depends on the case, publish the consultation fee and explain how you give an estimate before treatment starts.
  5. Book an appointment. A short form (name, phone, preferred day and time, and the reason in a few words) plus WhatsApp. You are dealing with health information, so do not ask for a medical history on a public form. Ask for it in the clinic.
  6. Contact and directions. Full address, a map link, landmarks, the floor and whether there is a lift, parking, timings, and what a patient should do after hours.
  7. Questions patients ask. Pain, number of visits, payment methods, whether you treat children, and anything your front desk answers every day.

Details that build trust

  • Real photographs of the reception, a treatment room and your sterilisation area. A stock photo of a smiling model tells a patient nothing about your clinic.
  • Hygiene in plain words. Describe how instruments are cleaned and sterilised. It is factual, and it answers a real question before the patient has to ask it.
  • Reviews that are real. Link to your Google reviews rather than copying a selection onto the site. Ask every patient the same way: Google's policy forbids offering incentives for reviews and selectively asking only happy patients.
  • Languages. If your team speaks Hindi or another language, say so. On a Delhi website a Hindi version can help many patients.

Speed and phones

Google says it "uses the mobile version of a site's content, crawled with the smartphone agent, for indexing and ranking". Build for the phone first: buttons large enough to tap, text readable without zooming, and photos compressed so the page opens quickly on mobile data.

Your website and your Google Business Profile

Your Google listing and your website work as a pair. Keep the clinic's name, address, phone number and timings identical on both. Google's guidelines say a business name should match how the business is known in the real world, without added keywords, and dentists who see patients directly may also have their own practitioner profiles.

Do not pay anyone who promises you the top spot. Google states: "There's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google." It adds that local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and popularity, and that how well known a business is depends partly on how many reviews it has and how many websites link to it.

The checklist

  • Name, locality, timings, call, WhatsApp and booking buttons, all visible on a phone without scrolling
  • One page for each main treatment
  • Dentists with degrees as registered, and specialist titles only where qualified
  • Fees or fee ranges, or a clear explanation of how estimates are given
  • A short booking form that does not ask for medical history
  • Address, map link, landmarks, timings and after-hours instructions
  • No "best", "No. 1" or "first" claims anywhere
  • Real clinic photos, and patient photos only with written consent
  • The same name, address, phone and timings on the website and your Google Business Profile
  • A site that opens quickly on mobile data

Questions clinic owners ask

Can a dental clinic show its fees on its website?

Yes. Clause 8.2.9 of the Dental Council of India's code says a website can carry details of treatment facilities and their fees.

Can we call ourselves the best dental clinic in the area?

No. The code treats a claim of superiority over others as unethical (clause 8.2.8) and rules out boastful claims of being the "best" or "first" (clause 8.2.7). Describe what you do and how, and let patients compare.

Do we need a separate page for each treatment?

For your main treatments, yes. A patient searching for one treatment wants that treatment's details, and a dedicated page answers them far better than a list on the home page.

What does a dental clinic website cost?

With us, a website of several pages costs ₹12,000 to ₹25,000, paid once. The Growth plan, with a page for each treatment, a booking form and a Hindi version, is ₹1,999/month + ₹2,999 one-time setup, on a 12-month plan. Our guide to what a website costs in India covers the rest, including the yearly costs.

We build websites for dental clinics in Delhi and across India. See what a dental clinic website from us includes, or send us your clinic's details and we will reply with a written scope and price.

title: School Website Requirements: CBSE Disclosure and Admissions
description: What a school website in India needs: CBSE's mandatory public disclosure, the pages parents check before admission, and a checklist to finish by November.
content:
A school website has two jobs. It has to satisfy your board, which for a CBSE school means publishing a mandatory public disclosure on the website. And it has to help with admissions, which means answering a parent's questions quickly and clearly, on a phone, while they compare you with other schools.

This guide covers both jobs, with a checklist to finish before the admission season starts.

What CBSE requires on a school website

CBSE expects every affiliated school to run a website. Its affiliation FAQ asks "Is it mandatory for schools to maintain website?" and answers: "Yes, the schools are required to develop and maintain its website providing vital information about the school on the website."

That vital information is the Mandatory Public Disclosure, in the Appendix IX format (CBSE Circulars 03/2021 of 5 March 2021 and 09/2021 of 21 May 2021, and their later amendments). In January 2026, CBSE told affiliated schools to upload the disclosure in its revised format by 15 February 2026 and warned that non-compliance could lead to action under the affiliation bye-laws, as Careers360 and Education Post reported.

The format has five parts: general information, documents and information, result and academics, teaching staff, and school infrastructure. According to Careers360's report of the 2026 circular, schools must publish, among other things:

  • The fee structure and the annual academic calendar
  • School Management Committee (SMC) and Parent-Teacher Association (PTA) details
  • Class 10 and Class 12 board results for the last three years
  • The number of registered students, and the teacher-student ratio
  • Teachers' details and qualifications: principal, vice-principal, PGTs, TGTs, PRTs, special educators and counsellors
  • Self-attested documents: affiliation and renewal letters, trust or society registration, RTE recognition, building and fire safety certificates, drinking water and sanitation certificates, and the DEO certificate

Put the disclosure behind a clearly labelled "Mandatory Public Disclosure" link on the home page, keep every document current, and replace a certificate on the day it is renewed. If your school follows a state board or ICSE, check that board's own rules. The admission advice below applies to every school.

The pages parents check before admission

Assume a parent is reading on a phone, comparing you with two or three other schools. Give them these pages:

  1. Admissions. The most important page in the season. It should say which classes are open, the age criteria for each class as on a stated date, the process step by step (registration, form, interaction if any, list, fee payment), the documents required, and the important dates for this year. Add an enquiry form and a WhatsApp button.
  2. Fee structure. A clear table by class, separating one-time, annual and termly or monthly charges, with transport shown on its own. For a CBSE school this is part of the disclosure anyway.
  3. Academics. The curriculum, the subjects and streams offered in Classes 11 and 12, and how students are assessed.
  4. Facilities. Labs, library, sports and activity spaces, shown in real photographs of your campus.
  5. Transport. Routes or areas covered, pick-up and drop timings, and the fee.
  6. Notices and calendar. Holidays, parent-teacher meetings and exam dates. A notices section with last year's dates on it tells parents nobody is looking after the site.
  7. Results and achievements. Board results as published. Show a student's name or photograph only with the parents' consent.
  8. Contact. Office timings, phone, WhatsApp, email, a map link, and which gate visitors should use.

When to have it ready

Admission seasons start early. In Delhi, registration for nursery and other entry-level classes in private unaided schools for the 2026-27 session opened on 4 December 2025, with the first list scheduled for 23 January 2026, according to the Directorate of Education schedule reported by Careers360. Parents need your details before forms open, so aim to have the admissions page, the fee structure and the enquiry form live by November.

Handling admission enquiries

A website that collects enquiries is only as good as what happens next:

  • Keep the form short. Parent's name, phone number, the class sought and an optional message. Ask for more at the school, not on a public form.
  • Reply within one working day, on the channel the parent used.
  • Keep one list of every enquiry with its status, so nobody is forgotten in the rush.
  • Show the next step. After a form is sent, tell the parent what will happen and when.

Speed, phones and Google

Google says it "uses the mobile version of a site's content, crawled with the smartphone agent, for indexing and ranking". So the phone version of your site is the one that counts: readable text without zooming, buttons large enough to tap, and photos compressed so the page opens quickly on mobile data.

Your Google Business Profile matters as much as the website when a parent searches for schools nearby. Keep the school's name, address, phone number and office timings the same on both, and use the school's real name without added keywords, as Google's guidelines require.

The checklist

  • A "Mandatory Public Disclosure" link on the home page, in the current Appendix IX format, with documents in date (CBSE schools)
  • An admissions page with classes, age criteria, process, documents and this year's dates
  • A fee table by class, with transport separate
  • An enquiry form and a WhatsApp button on every page
  • Academics, facilities and transport pages with real photographs
  • Notices and a calendar that are actually current
  • Results as published, and student photos only with consent
  • Contact details, office timings and a map link
  • The same name, address and phone on the website and your Google Business Profile
  • Everything above live by November

Questions school owners ask

Is a website compulsory for a CBSE school?

Yes. CBSE's affiliation FAQ says schools are required to develop and maintain a website, and the Mandatory Public Disclosure in the Appendix IX format has to be published on it.

What is the Mandatory Public Disclosure?

A set of information and documents that CBSE requires an affiliated school to publish on its website: general information, documents and certificates, results and academics, teaching staff, and infrastructure.

Should a school put its fees on the website?

For a CBSE school, the fee structure is part of the disclosure. For any school, a clear fee table saves parents a phone call and saves your office from answering the same question all season.

How much does a school website cost?

With us, a school website of several pages costs ₹12,000 to ₹25,000, paid once. On a monthly plan, Growth is ₹1,999/month + ₹2,999 one-time setup, on a 12-month plan, and adds a page for each course or service, an enquiry form and a Hindi version. Our guide to what a website costs in India covers the yearly costs too.

See what a school website from us includes, or send us your school's details for a written scope and a fixed price.

title: Coaching Institute Website: What to Show and What to Avoid
description: What a coaching institute website should show students and parents, what the 2024 guidelines ask for, and how to publish results without misleading anyone.
content:
A student choosing a coaching institute, and the parent who pays for it, want the same few facts. Which courses do you run? When does the next batch start? Who teaches? What does it cost, and what happens if the student has to leave? Where are you, exactly? A coaching website that answers these plainly does more for admissions than one that shouts about toppers.

There is a rulebook side too. In 2024 the Ministry of Education sent states guidelines for regulating coaching centres, and the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) issued guidelines on misleading coaching advertisements. Both shape what your website should say, and what it should not.

The pages students and parents look for

  1. A page for each course. The exam or class it prepares for, who can join, the duration, what the syllabus covers, batch timings and start dates, classroom or online, the fee with its instalments, and what is included, such as study material and tests.
  2. Batches and timetable. The next start dates, weekday and weekend options, and how to join a batch already running.
  3. Faculty. Each teacher's name, subject and qualifications, stated as they are.
  4. Fees and refunds. The total fee for each course, the instalment plan, and your refund policy in writing.
  5. Results. Built carefully, following the rules further down.
  6. Demo class or counselling session. How to book one, how long it lasts, and what to bring.
  7. Contact. Address with landmarks, a map link, timings, phone and WhatsApp. Students and parents weigh travel time, so make the location impossible to miss.

What the 2024 coaching guidelines ask a website to show

The Ministry of Education's Guidelines for Regulation of Coaching Centre, 2024 were sent to states and union territories to adopt through their own legal framework, so check what your state has actually notified. Among the conditions they propose, according to published summaries of the guidelines, is a website with updated details of:

  • the qualifications of tutors
  • the courses and curriculum, and how long each takes to complete
  • hostel facilities, if any
  • the fees being charged
  • the exit policy and the fee refund policy
  • how many students took coaching at the centre, and how many went on to get admission in higher education institutions

The same summaries describe other conditions worth knowing about: tutors should be at least graduates, students below 16 should not be enrolled, and a student who has paid in full and leaves mid-course should get a pro-rata refund for the remaining period within 10 days. Even where your state has not adopted the guidelines, a website that already shows this information answers a careful parent's questions before they are asked.

How to show results without misleading anyone

The CCPA's Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisement in Coaching Sector, 2024 were announced on 13 November 2024. They apply to everyone engaged in coaching, endorsers included, and define a coaching centre as one that coaches more than fifty students. For the results on your website, the main points in the government's announcement are:

  • No false claims about selections, ranks, success rates, courses, faculty, fees or refund policies.
  • No guarantees of selection, admission or high scores.
  • Consent after success. A student's name, photo or testimonial may be used only with their written consent, taken after their success, not at enrolment.
  • Full details beside the photo. The student's name, rank and course details, and whether the course was paid for.
  • No fine print. Disclaimers in the same font size as the other important details.
  • No false urgency. Do not claim limited seats or rush demand that is not real.

In practice, build the results page as a table rather than a collage. One row per student who has consented, with the exam, the year, the rank or score as published, the course they took, how long it ran, and whether it was paid, a scholarship or free. To a careful parent it reads as more honest than a wall of photographs, and it keeps you inside the rules.

One more point from the Ministry's guidelines, as summarised: results of the institute's own internal tests should not be made public. Keep test toppers off the website and use those scores for teaching.

Turning visits into enquiries

  • WhatsApp on every page, so a student can ask a question without having to make a call.
  • A demo-class form that asks only for the student's name, class, course of interest and a phone number.
  • Batch dates in plain view. If a batch is full, say so honestly and show the next one.
  • Reply the same day during admission season, while the family is still comparing institutes.
  • A fee page with instalments, so a family can check affordability before calling.

If your main intake comes in spring, after the board exams, have the course pages, fees and batch dates live by January or February, so the pages are found and trusted before families start comparing.

Speed and phones

Assume your students open the site on a phone, on mobile data. Google says it "uses the mobile version of a site's content, crawled with the smartphone agent, for indexing and ranking", so the phone version is the one that counts for search too. Keep pages light, text readable without zooming and buttons large enough to tap.

The checklist

  • A page for each course, with eligibility, duration, timings, fee and inclusions
  • Next batch dates, and a way to join a running batch
  • Faculty with real qualifications
  • Fees, instalments and a written refund policy
  • A results table with consent, course details and paid or free status, and no internal test results
  • No guaranteed selections, no false "limited seats"
  • WhatsApp and a short demo-class form on every page
  • Address, landmarks, map link and timings
  • Fast on a phone

Questions coaching owners ask

Can we put toppers' photos on our website?

Only with the student's written consent, taken after their success, and with their name, rank, course details and whether the course was paid shown alongside, under the CCPA's 2024 guidelines.

Do we have to show fees on the website?

The Ministry of Education's guidelines propose that a coaching centre's website show the fees charged and the refund policy. Check what your state has adopted. Either way, a clear fee page saves your counsellors from answering the same question all day.

Can we write "limited seats" on the website?

Only if it is true. The CCPA guidelines treat false urgency and false scarcity as misleading.

What does a coaching institute website cost?

With us, a website of several pages costs ₹12,000 to ₹25,000, paid once. The Growth plan, with a page for each course, an enquiry form and a Hindi version, is ₹1,999/month + ₹2,999 one-time setup, on a 12-month plan. More detail in what a website costs in India.

We built the website for HighQ Classes, a coaching institute: read how it was put together. See what a coaching institute website from us includes, or tell us about your institute for a written scope and price.

title: Monthly Website Plan or One-Time Payment: Which to Choose?
description: A website on a monthly plan or bought outright? First-year costs side by side, who owns what, how changes work, and five questions to ask any provider.
content:
There are two ways to pay for a business website. You can buy it outright: a fixed price, paid once, and the site is yours. Or you can take a monthly plan: a setup fee, then a monthly fee, and the provider builds, hosts and looks after the site for you.

Neither is always cheaper. Which one suits you depends on how much you want to spend up front, how often the site needs changing, and how much you care about owning the code. This guide puts real numbers on both, using our own prices from October 2026.

How a one-time website works

You agree a scope and a fixed price. With us you pay 50% in advance and 50% at launch, and the custom code is yours on the final payment. After launch you pay for hosting and your domain yourself, in your own name. You update the site yourself where it has editable areas, or pay someone to do it; our care plans for that start at ₹1,000 a month.

How a monthly website plan works

You pay a one-time setup fee, then a monthly fee for a fixed term. The provider builds your site on a ready design, puts in your logo, text and photos, hosts it, keeps it running and makes a set number of small changes each month.

Our two plans:

  • Starter: ₹899/month + ₹2,999 one-time setup, on a 12-month plan. A website on one of our ready designs (up to 5 pages), a WhatsApp button, hosting and SSL, 2 content changes a month and support on WhatsApp.
  • Growth: ₹1,999/month + ₹2,999 one-time setup, on a 12-month plan. Everything in Starter, plus a page for each treatment, course or service, a booking or enquiry form, a Hindi version and 5 content changes a month.

Your domain is registered in your name and paid by you to the registrar. The text, photos and logo you supply stay yours. The website itself, its design and code, is licensed to you while the plan runs, and you can buy it out: the buy-out price is written into your plan before you pay the setup fee.

What about the second and third year?

Over three years, if the Starter plan carries on at today's price, it comes to ₹35,363 (₹2,999 + 36 × ₹899), with hosting and changes included, and the site is still licensed rather than owned. A one-time website costs ₹12,000 to ₹25,000 once, plus your own hosting and domain every year, and it is yours. Add our lowest care plan and three years of care alone comes to ₹36,000.

So neither option wins on price alone. You are really choosing two things: who does the upkeep, and whether you pay up front or as you go.

A monthly plan suits you if

  • You would rather not pay ₹12,000 or more in one go.
  • You do not want to deal with hosting, renewals or security certificates.
  • Your fees, timings, notices or offers change most months.
  • A ready design with your own logo, text and photos is enough for now.

A one-time website suits you if

  • You want to own the site and its code outright.
  • You need a custom design, or features a plan does not include.
  • The site will rarely change, or someone on your team can update it.
  • You already pay for hosting, or want to choose your own.

Five questions to ask any monthly website offer

Monthly offers are easy to compare badly, because the monthly figure is the smallest number on the page. Before you sign any plan, from us or from anyone else, get written answers to these:

  1. What is the setup fee, and how long is the term? A monthly price shown without them hides part of the cost. India's Central Consumer Protection Authority lists "drip pricing", where parts of a price are not revealed upfront, among 13 dark patterns in its 2023 guidelines.
  2. What does stopping early cost, if anything?
  3. What is the buy-out price if you want to keep the site?
  4. Is the domain registered in your name, on your own account? If the provider owns your domain, leaving can mean losing your address.
  5. What counts as a change? With us, a change is one small edit you send on WhatsApp: a new photo, a price or timing update, a new notice, a corrected line of text. A new page, a new section or a new feature is quoted first, and nothing is done until you agree.

Also ask what happens at the end of the term: whether the plan renews on its own, and at what price. Our answers to all of these are on our pricing page.

Questions people ask

Is a monthly website plan the same as renting a website?

Close. You pay to use a site that the provider hosts and maintains, while your domain and your content stay yours. On our plans you can also buy the site out and own it.

Can I move from a monthly plan to owning the site?

Yes, by buying it out. The buy-out price is written into your plan before you pay the setup fee, so you know it from the first day.

Can I cancel a monthly plan?

With us, you tell us on WhatsApp. The plan is for 12 months, and what stopping early costs, if anything, is written into your plan before you pay the setup fee. When a plan ends the website comes down unless you buy it out, and your domain, text and photos stay yours.

Which is better for a clinic, a school or a coaching institute?

If you have several treatments or courses and want enquiries through the site, both the Growth plan and a one-time multi-page website work.
